data.text/markdown:
IEX · what the free feed holds, and what a strategy could take from it

IEX (Investors Exchange) is one US stock exchange, about 2-3% of US share volume. Its free HIST download is its DEEP market-data feed of a past trading day, for the whole market, a day late: every change of its displayed order book, every trade, and the status of every stock. This notebook opens one day of it and shows, with pictures, what each kind of message holds (§1-§3), what information a strategy could extract and how each piece is computed (§4), and what testing that would cost (§5). In four lines:
  • The book is IEX's own, displayed orders only, summed per price: no single orders, no queue positions, no hidden liquidity. It is thin and often many ticks wide.
  • The trades are every execution on IEX, hidden liquidity included, with flags (intermarket sweep, odd lot, extended hours ...) but no buy / sell side. Many print inside the displayed spread.
  • The status messages cover about 13,000 symbols at once: halts, the short-sale restriction (Rule 201), IEX's opening, a retail-interest flag. This is the part that bars cannot give you.
  • Auctions and official prices exist only for IEX-listed securities. In the file you load, those are test symbols.
How to use it. Run it with uv run marimo edit strategies/orderbook/iex_data_explained_marimo.py (or the VS Code marimo extension). §1 asks for a day and a click: the first MB of the day's file are downloaded (a stored file is not fetched again) and decoded, about a minute the first time. From §3 on, the pictures react to the controls above them: the stock, the width of the ladder, the moment drawn in Fig 4, the bucket of Fig 5. Code: iex_features.py and orderbook_free.py (tests: tests/test_iex_features.py, tests/test_orderbook_free.py). Data: var/orderbook_free/ (git-ignored; IEX's historical data is under IEX's terms of use). The message formats are IEX's DEEP specification v1.08. Nothing here is a trading result: no feature below has been tested for predicting returns.

1 · What IEX gives away for free

IEX's file index (iextrading.com/api/1.0/hist) lists, for each trading day, a capture of each feed: TOPS (best bid and offer, last sale), DEEP (the price-level book, trades, status messages) and the newer DPLS / DPLC files (from 2024 and 2026; presumably the order-by-order DEEP+, not opened here). They are next-day, free, and large: the tables count them and size them. One technical fact decides what is cheap: a gzip file can only be read from its START, so the opening of a day is cheap (a prefix) while its afternoon and close cost the whole file.

data.text/markdown: 2026-10-19: IEX's DEEP file for the day is 12.0 GB; the first 200 MB are used here (downloaded in 19 s). Decoded 6,779,500 messages in 14 s (0.47 M per second) from a pcapng capture. System events (New York): start of messages 07:06:52, system hours 08:00:00, regular hours 09:30:00. Book updates run from 08:00:00 to 09:32:54; 11,097 symbols had at least one. Books rebuilt for: INTC, SPY, NVDA, AAPL.

2 · What is inside one DEEP day

The capture is a stream of small binary messages. The table lists every message type, what it tells you, which securities it covers, and how many there are in the part of the file you fetched: nearly all are price-level updates (the displayed size at one price changed); trades and status messages are about one percent each. Fig 1 is the feed's pulse: the start-of-day status spin, the quiet pre-market, and the burst when the regular session starts and every book is rebuilt at once.

data.text/markdown: Reading Fig 1. Each line counts one kind of message per 10-second bucket, on a log scale. The status messages come in one wave before 08:00 (every symbol's trading status, operational halt, short-sale status and retail flag) and again at 09:30:00, when each stock's opening completes. Book updates trickle in from 08:00, then jump by two to three orders of magnitude at 09:30:00: IEX publishes the whole queued book of every stock within a second. Trades follow the same shape. After the first seconds the rate settles at a level far above the pre-market's.

3 · One stock's book, as a picture

Fig 2 is the DEEP book of one stock from a few seconds before to about a minute after the open. Price runs up, time across, and the colour is the shares resting at that price (blue = bids, orange = asks, darker = more). The dark lines are the best bid and ask, the grey dots are trades on IEX. Look for three things: (1) the left edge, before 09:30:00: how much book is there near the market?; (2) how fast the book appears at the open; (3) how sparse and uneven it is: a few levels, gaps, a spread of several ticks. DEEP shows displayed orders only, summed per price: one 300-share order and three 100-share orders look the same, and hidden or midpoint-peg liquidity does not appear at all, although it trades (§4.4). The controls choose the stock (for this figure and all that follow) and how many ticks around the mid the ladder keeps (a stock with a wide book, such as SPY, needs a larger number).

data.text/markdown:
4 · What a strategy could extract, and how each piece is computed

Five kinds of information come out of the feed. For each: how it is computed (with a picture of the calculation on real data), what a strategy could use it for, and what limits it here. The pointers (author, year) are where the idea comes from; they were not checked for this notebook.

4.1 · Liquidity state: spread and depth

How it is computed. From the book after every update: the quoted spread is (best ask − best bid) / mid, in basis points; depth is the dollar value (price × shares) resting within 10 bps of the mid, both sides together. Both are sampled every second. Use: a cost estimate (a strategy that trades at the touch pays about half the spread each way), an entry filter (skip names whose book is wide or thin), execution timing (Fig 3 shows how the book builds after the open), a regime variable for other signals. Limit: this is IEX's book, not the market's: the consolidated spread is usually tighter. The table compares the stocks before and after the open.

data.text/markdown:
4.2 · Queue imbalance and microprice

How they are computed (the left half of Fig 4 draws them on one real instant). With Qb and Qa the shares queued at the best bid and ask:
  • queue imbalance OBI(1) = (Qb − Qa) / (Qb + Qa), in [−1, +1]: +1 means only bids are queued at the touch, −1 only asks. OBI(3) (the setting LEVELS) uses the sizes of the best three levels per side.
  • microprice (bid × Qa + ask × Qb) / (Qb + Qa): the mid, pulled toward the side with LESS size, because a thin queue is exhausted first and the price tends to step that way.
Use: a forecast of the next price move over seconds. Published work finds that queue imbalance helps forecast the next move (Lipton, Pesavento & Sotiropoulos 2013, mainly for large-tick stocks; Cao, Hansch & Wang 2009; Stoikov 2018). Limit: it fades within seconds, so spread and fees decide whether anything survives; and these are IEX's queues, a few percent of the market's. The instant in Fig 4 is, by default, the most lopsided queue in the first minute (so the formula has something to show): it is not a typical moment. Switch the automatic pick off to choose the moment yourself. The right half shows how the same quantities move around it.

4.3 · Order-flow imbalance (OFI)

How it is computed (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov 2014). Compare each new best-bid / best-ask state with the one before. A bid that is higher or equal adds its whole size to buying pressure; a bid that is lower or equal takes the old size away (at an unchanged price both apply, so the net is the change of size); asks work the mirror way (an ask that is lifted away or shrunk is buying pressure). The first table applies the rule to six consecutive real states, starting at the moment of Fig 4 (e_bid + e_ask = ofi). Then OFI is summed over short buckets and set against the change of the mid over the same bucket (Fig 5); the bucket length is a control. Use: it explains the price change of the same interval (price impact: the slope is roughly inverse to the depth), and is an input to impact models and short-horizon forecasts. That is a description, not a forecast: whether one bucket's OFI predicts the NEXT bucket's move is a separate question that this notebook does not answer. Limit: the last table shows that even the same-interval relation depends on the bucket length and on the stock, and is clearest in the shortest buckets (the long buckets have few observations: see the noise band printed under the table).

data.text/markdown:
4.4 · Trades: where they print, and who pushed

DEEP's trade report has price, size and flags, but not the side. A trade is labelled buyer- or seller-initiated by comparing its price with the IEX quote just before it (Lee & Ready 1991): at the ask or above the mid = buy, at the bid or below the mid = sell, exactly at the mid = the tick rule (the sign of the last price change). DEEP sends a trade report before the book update it causes, with the same timestamp, so the quote used must be strictly earlier. Table 1 says where trades print against IEX's own quote: a trade inside the displayed spread executed against liquidity the book does not show (midpoint or hidden orders). Table 2 counts the flags over every stock after the open. Fig 6 shows the chosen stock's trades labelled this way, and the running total of signed shares. Use: signed volume per interval (order-flow pressure; cf. Chordia & Subrahmanyam 2004), the share of intermarket sweeps (urgent, liquidity-taking orders), odd-lot activity, trades per second as an activity measure. Volume-bucketed versions of signed flow have been proposed as a "toxicity" measure (VPIN; Easley, López de Prado & O'Hara 2012; disputed). Limit: IEX's trades are a small part of the market; the sign is inferred; and a print at the midpoint says little about direction.

data.text/markdown:
4.5 · Market-wide status: halts, short-sale restriction, the opening, retail interest

These messages are published for every symbol, so one file gives a cross-section of about 13,000 names, not four. Each symbol gets a status "spin" before 08:00, then a message whenever something changes:
  • Short sale price test (Reg SHO rule 201): in effect once a stock has fallen 10% from its previous close; the restriction lasts the rest of that day and the next. Names already restricted at the start of the day are recent big losers; names switched on after 09:30:00 are stocks trading at least 10% below yesterday's close right now, stamped to the millisecond.
  • Trading status: H = halted across all US markets (reason NA for names not listed on IEX), T = trading. A halt and its release are events.
  • Operational halt: halted on IEX only. Security event O: IEX has finished opening the stock's book.
  • Retail liquidity indicator: A / B / C when IEX holds retail-eligible buy / sell / both-side interest, blank otherwise. It says that interest exists; not how much, not at what price.
Use: event lists the instant the market opens (who gaps down 10%, who is halted and when it is released), a "do not trade" filter, and a cross-sectional retail-attention measure. Limit: only a few dozen events in the first minutes, so a test needs many days; and the retail flag's link to returns is not established.

data.text/markdown: What the auction and official-price messages hold. They exist only for IEX-listed securities, and the security directory (also IEX-listed only) says who that is. The tables below show the directory and what the auction and official-price messages say. If the directory lists only test securities (the test_security column), the auction information, the imbalance fields and the official prices carry nothing about real stocks. The auction schedule (information once a second from two minutes before the open) and the fields (paired shares, imbalance side and size, indicative price, collars) are what a closing-imbalance signal would use on an exchange with listed stocks.

data.text/markdown: Where I would look first (a judgement, not a result). (1) The status fields at the open: they are the only thing here that no bar data has, they span the whole market (thousands of names, so every kind of stock, though only a handful of events per day), and they sit in the first seconds of the file, which is the cheap part. (2) Opening-minute book and trade features (spread, depth, signed flow over the first 1-3 minutes) against the following 5-30 minutes' returns, which the repo's 1-minute bars in the database could supply for about 1,750 names. (3) Tick-level imbalance and OFI strategies last: they need full-day files, they see only IEX's thin book, and seconds-long edges meet the spread. The next table puts numbers on the cost.
